strengths: Addresses an important problem: causal discovery in irregular, incomplete time series is highly relevant to healthcare, finance, and climate science
Well-motivated approach with clear illustrations (Figure 1) of why existing impute-then-discover and alignment-based methods fail
Conceptually sound joint EM framework that unifies imputation and structure learning, addressing a real gap in existing methods
Supports both linear and nonlinear causal mechanisms through kernel-based regression
Provides asymptotic consistency guarantees (Proposition 1) under standard assumptions
Strong synthetic experimental results showing robustness under 60-80% missingness (F1=1.0 vs 0.2 for CUTS+)
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical framework carefully develops kernel-based methods in RKHS, but implementation uses neural networks with no connection between the two. Section 4.4.1 explicitly departs from classical EM, undermining whether Proposition 1's convergence guarantees apply to actual implementation
Convergence analysis lacks finite-sample bounds and rates for the implemented neural-network version; only asymptotic guarantees provided
Kernel projection mechanism (Eq. 4) insufficiently justified: Φk,j is never defined or computed, making claimed interpretability unsubstantiated
Severely limited real-world validation: only one dataset (10-node CausalRivers subgraph) with simulated missingness; no evaluation on actual irregularly-sampled time series from target domains

Unfair baseline comparisons: (1) all baselines receive TimeMixer preprocessing while ReTimeCausal handles missingness natively, (2) CUTS+ failure (F1≈0.2 vs 1.0) is unexplained and suspicious, (3) MissDAG omitted despite being most similar work

Noise-aware imputation (Section 4.3) lacks empirical validation; no ablation study demonstrates its contribution; circular dependency between residual distribution estimation and parameter updates is unaddressed

Substantial missing implementation details: hyperparameter selection procedures (λ, γ, α, σ) not described, neural network architectures unspecified, convergence criteria unclear, no computational complexity or runtime analysis
No ablation studies: impossible to determine which components (EM, kernels, noise injection, pruning) drive performance improvements
Experimental design does not validate core motivation: uses random MCAR on regular grids, not true irregular sampling with variable time intervals; timestamp handling unclear

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming (ReCausalTime vs ReTimeCausal), kernel formulation claims non-additive interactions contradicting additive noise assumption, typos (conbributions, exhibit irregular)
Standard deviation reporting inconsistency: claims std<0.001 but Table 3 shows error bars up to ±0.0980
Restrictive assumptions (time-invariant mechanisms, causal sufficiency, no unmeasured confounders) with no robustness analysis when violated

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: causal discovery in irregular time series with missing data
Clear and well-illustrated motivation showing limitations of impute-then-discover and alignment-based pipelines
Principled approach combining EM, Additive Noise Models, and kernel regression
Supports both linear and nonlinear causal mechanisms
Strong empirical performance on synthetic data, especially at high missingness rates (80% missing → F1=1.0)
Correctly identifies and addresses the issue of deterministic imputation violating pruning assumptions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: EM+ANM for missing data already explored by MissDAG (2022); differences not clearly articulated
Theoretical contribution is weak: Proposition 1 provides only asymptotic consistency (n,k→∞) without finite-sample guarantees or convergence rates
Strong assumptions undermine applicability: Causal Sufficiency (Assumption 3.4) is rarely satisfied in practice; no robustness analysis for confounders

Methodology has significant gaps: (1) Structure learning operator S(·) vaguely defined; (2) kernel projection (Eq. 4) lacks theoretical justification for preserving causal semantics; (3) noise-aware imputation (Eq. 7) appears circular and ad-hoc
Misleading EM framing: Section 4.4.2 admits using direct neural optimization rather than true EM, contradicting the main narrative

Experimental evaluation severely limited: only 1 real dataset (10 nodes, 19 edges); no experiments on CUTS/CUTS+ benchmarks; suspicious poor performance of CUTS+ suggests potential implementation issues
Unfair baseline comparisons: ReTimeCausal can refine imputations iteratively while baselines see only fixed TimeMixer output, creating structural advantage
Critical implementation details missing: no hyperparameter selection methodology (λ, γ, α, σ, L); convergence criterion unspecified; network architecture undefined; insufficient statistical reporting
Identifiability not addressed: when is the causal graph recoverable? How do kernel approximations affect identifiability?

Irregular sampling claims overstated: method doesn't explicitly model temporal irregularity or sampling times; kernel operates on values X^t, not timestamps; primarily handles missing data, not true irregular sampling
Simple synthetic nonlinearities don't reflect real-world complexity: element-wise transformations (sin, tanh) are not representative of complex nonlinear systems
Reproducibility concerns: insufficient details for implementation; no code provided; many design choices lack justification

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in existing approaches (impute-then-discover and temporal alignment methods) through effective illustrations
Principled integration of EM and ANM for jointly optimizing imputation and structure learning rather than treating sequentially

Impressive synthetic experimental results with significant improvements over baselines under severe missingness (F1=1.0 on 20-variable setting with 80% missing data; F1=0.816 on 50-variable nonlinear setting)
Thoughtful solution to CAM independence assumptions through noise-aware imputation strategy (Eq. 7) that explicitly injects noise during data completion
Comprehensive methodological framework addressing multiple challenges: nonlinearity via kernel regression, interpretability through sparsity constraints, and structure-aware imputation
Theoretical grounding with Proposition 1 establishing structural consistency under standard assumptions
Generally clear presentation with effective motivation and intuitive explanations of key challenges
weaknesses: Critical contradiction between claimed approach and implementation: paper claims to avoid 'black-box neural networks' for interpretability but Section 4.4.1 reveals functions are parameterized as neural networks. The relationship between kernel-based formulation (Section 4.2) and neural network parameterization (Section 4.4.1) is confusing and poorly integrated

Noise-aware imputation (Section 4.3) is severely under-specified: unclear which residuals are used, how residual distribution is estimated in early EM iterations, and whether noise sampling at each iteration introduces excessive variance into final causal graph estimates

Severely limited real-world validation: only one dataset (CausalRivers) with single 10-node subgraph tested. Claim of 'extensive empirical validation' unjustified given motivating examples are healthcare, finance, climate science but no datasets from these domains

Theoretical analysis limited to asymptotic consistency: Proposition 1 assumes infinite samples and sufficient iterations, providing no finite-sample guarantees relevant to practical settings. Proof sketch missing (relegated to appendix not provided), preventing verification

Neural network + EM integration raises unaddressed concerns: combining EM with gradient-based neural network optimization (non-convex) may violate classical EM convergence guarantees. Identifiability with learned noise distributions unclear

Suspicious baseline performance: CUTS+ (designed for this exact setting) achieves F1≈0.21 even at 0% missing rate, suggesting either poor tuning/implementation or unfair comparison. CUTS+ significantly underperforms claims in its own paper

Missing critical implementation details relegated to appendix (not provided): hyperparameter selection procedures (γ, α, λ), convergence criteria, EM initialization strategy, complete algorithm pseudocode, and pruning procedure all unavailable

Incomplete methodology description: paper claims EM framework but then states 'departing from classical formulation by using direct optimization with neural estimators,' leaving unclear what objective is actually being optimized

Strong unverified assumptions with limited discussion: Assumptions 3.2-3.4 (finite-order Markov, time-invariant mechanisms, causal sufficiency) are restrictive; MCAR/MAR assumption excludes realistic MNAR scenarios, acknowledged as future work

Experimental concerns: (1) Standard deviations reported as 'consistently below 0.001' but Table 3 shows std=0.0980; (2) No statistical significance testing despite reported small std; (3) Hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed; (4) No ablation studies

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance in healthcare, finance, and climate science; excellent problem illustration in Figure 1
Principled EM-based framework that is technically sound, combining neural imputation with kernel-based structure learning for flexibility and interpretability
Clever insight on noise-aware imputation (Section 4.3) to maintain independence assumptions required for pruning methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including synthetic datasets across varying conditions (20-80% missingness, 10-50 variables), ablation studies (noise injection, lag orders, R²-sortability), and multiple real-world benchmarks
Provides asymptotic consistency guarantees (Proposition 4.1) and finite-sample SHD bounds (Theorem G.1) extending classical results to irregular sampling settings
Honest discussion of limitations in Appendix L, including MNAR, instantaneous effects, and time-varying structures
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees are asymptotic only ('lim k→∞ lim n→∞'), providing limited practical assurance for finite samples that practitioners face; constants in Theorem G.1 are unspecified, raising questions about bound tightness

Significant theory-practice gap: the practical algorithm uses exponential smoothing, thresholding, CAM pruning, and neural network approximators that are not fully incorporated into theoretical convergence analysis; back-projection approximation (Eq. 5) magnitude and impact unquantified
Modest real-world improvements on CausalRivers: F1=0.463 vs. PCMCI+TimeMixer 0.414 (5% gain), F1=0.414 vs. CUTS+ 0.319 (6% gain); PCMCI+TimeMixer achieves better SHD; margins approach standard errors

Suspicious synthetic results: F1=1.000 at 80% missingness on linear-Gaussian data while baselines collapse to F1<0.2 raises overfitting concerns; CUTS+ (designed for irregular time series) underperforms dramatically without adequate explanation

Key design choices lack justification: why neural networks for E-step but kernels for M-step? How to choose discretization grid resolution (crucial for irregular sampling)? How to select lag order L in practice? Why exponential smoothing specifically?

Restrictive assumptions limit applicability: MCAR/MAR only (excludes MNAR common in healthcare/finance), causal sufficiency (no latent confounders), time-invariant causal directions (excludes distribution shift), no instantaneous effects

Computational complexity worst-case O(BT L² d³) for CAM pruning could be prohibitive for high-dimensional data; scalability to realistic large-scale problems unclear (primary real-world evaluation uses only 10-node subgraph)
Limited analysis of method failure modes, practical hyperparameter selection without ground truth, and interaction effects between multiple hyperparameters (α, β, γ, λ, p, L)

strengths: Addresses relevant problem of causal discovery with irregular sampling and missing data, important for healthcare, finance, and climate science
Well-motivated joint learning framework that integrates imputation and structure learning to address their interdependence
Thoughtful design choices like noise-aware imputation to preserve causal independence assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and multiple benchmarks in appendix
Provides formal theoretical analysis with consistency guarantees, though limited
Generally clear presentation with good use of motivating examples (Figure 1)
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantee (Proposition 4.1) is very weak: asymptotic-only with problematic double limit (lim_k→∞ lim_n→∞) assuming infinite iterations before sample limits; finite-sample Theorem G.1 lacks practical guidance with vacuous bounds when margin η is small

Real-world improvements are modest: only 11% relative F1 improvement on CausalRivers (0.463 vs 0.414), and ReTimeCausal doesn't achieve best SHD; paper acknowledges performance is modest; typical ICML improvements are >20%
Departs significantly from classical EM (neural E-step, kernel M-step graph recovery) without rigorous theoretical justification for why this should converge to true structure

Restrictive assumptions severely limit applicability: ignores MNAR (common in healthcare/finance), disallows instantaneous effects, assumes time-invariant causal graphs, and assumes causal sufficiency; Definition 3.1 contradicts Assumption 3.3

Suspicious synthetic results: perfect F1=1.0 under 80% missingness in Table 1 is unrealistic; standard deviations <0.001 suggest over-tuning; all baselines collapse suggesting data may be favorable to method

Noise injection mechanism (Eq. 8) lacks theoretical justification: no proof that sampling noise from residuals preserves independence; ablation shows dramatic impact (F1: 0.976→0.159) but theory is missing
Kernel back-projection (Eq. 5) is approximate not exact: how large is approximation error? How does it propagate through iterations? Unquantified uncertainty.
Inadequate comparison with most similar baseline CUTS+: ReTimeCausal uses classical regression vs CUTS+ neural RNNs; why should classical methods outperform neural? Advantage unclear
Algorithm and key design justifications relegated to appendix (Algorithm 1, ablations on noise injection and lag analysis); 9-page main paper + 18-page appendix indicates poor prioritization
Computational complexity concerning: worst-case O(d³) CAM pruning term dominates for moderate d; no runtime comparisons with baselines; scalability to high-dimensional problems unclear
Limited real-world evaluation: only 1 dataset (10-node CausalRivers) in main paper; appendix benchmarks are still small-scale; no evaluation on large climate/financial/genomic networks
Exponential smoothing (Eq. 9) and CAM application lack justification: no explanation for α choice or how smoothing affects theoretical guarantees; CAM designed for static data, not lagged settings
Hyperparameter selection not principled: Table 12 provides settings but no guidance for new problems; appendix shows sensitivity (F1 ranges 0.883-0.964 with β,γ variations)
Missing comparisons: no comparison with other EM-based structure learning, FCI/GES, or recent neural causal discovery methods; limited justification for baseline selection

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear concrete examples of failure modes in existing approaches (Figure 1)
Principled EM framework elegantly capturing interdependence between imputation and structure learning
Novel noise-aware imputation strategy (Eq. 8) solving the independence violation problem for CAM pruning
Theoretical contributions extending consistency guarantees to irregular sampling + high missingness settings, with both asymptotic (Prop. 4.1) and finite-sample (Thm. G.1) results
Comprehensive empirical validation: strong synthetic performance (F1=1.0 at 80% missingness), scalability to 50 variables, extensive ablations, multiple real-world benchmarks
Flexible framework supporting both linear and nonlinear mechanisms within unified ANM formulation
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation (Appendix K), algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, transparent limitations
Hyperparameter robustness demonstrated across wide ranges (α ∈ [0.7, 0.9], β ∈ [0.01, 0.10])
Clear presentation with logical organization from motivation through theory to experiments
weaknesses: Asymptotic nature of theoretical guarantees (limk→∞ limn→∞) with acknowledged gap between idealized theory and practical algorithm using neural networks, finite RFF approximations, and back-projection
Modest real-world improvements: F1 of 0.463 vs 0.414 for best baseline on CausalRivers (~5 percentage points), though consistent across benchmarks
Limited real-world evaluation: primarily single main real dataset (CausalRivers); additional benchmarks only in appendix; only 10-node graphs tested; SHD performance not best on real data

Strong assumptions restricting applicability: (1) MCAR/MAR missingness excludes MNAR common in healthcare/finance, (2) causal sufficiency rules out unobserved confounders, (3) no instantaneous effects limits high-frequency applications, (4) time-invariant causal directions precludes time-varying structures
Computational complexity O(BT L²d³) for CAM pruning potentially prohibitive for high-dimensional settings; no runtime comparisons provided; E-step scalability unclear as dimensions grow
Ad-hoc thresholding parameter γ selection (Eq. 7) lacks principled guidance despite ablation studies; hyperparameter variation across datasets (Table 12) raises questions about transferability
Noise injection via empirical residual distribution could propagate errors if early structural function estimates are poor, yet this risk is not analyzed
Noise-aware imputation mechanism novel but only justified via ablation (Table 5: F1 drops from 0.976 to 0.159 without it); theoretical understanding incomplete
No statistical significance testing despite claiming std < 0.001; no confidence intervals or p-values; fairness of TimeMixer preprocessing for baselines unclear
Gap between F1 improvements and SID performance on real data (F1=0.463 but SID=8.0) suggests edge detection doesn't translate to interventional fidelity; not explained
